pumac-2021-finals-a-01.title: Order of $n$ modulo $p$
pumac-2021-finals-a-01.body:
Suppose a prime $p=6k+5$ divides $n^2-n+1$. Since $n^3+1=(n+1)(n^2-n+1)$, we get $n^3\equiv-1\pmod p$, hence $n^6\equiv1\pmod p$ and $p\nmid n$. Let $d$ be the multiplicative order of $n$ modulo $p$. Then $d\mid6$ and $d\mid p-1$ (Fermat), so $d\mid\gcd(6,p-1)$. As $p-1=6k+4\equiv4\pmod6$, $\gcd(6,p-1)=2$, hence $d\in\{1,2\}$, i.e. $n^2\equiv1\pmod p$ and $n\equiv\pm1\pmod p$.

- If $n\equiv1$: $n^2-n+1\equiv1\not\equiv0$.
- If $n\equiv-1$: $n^2-n+1\equiv3\pmod p$, so $p\mid3$, i.e. $p=3$, but $3\not\equiv5\pmod6$.

Either way we reach a contradiction, so no prime of the form $6k+5$ divides $n^2-n+1$. $\blacksquare$

pumac-2021-finals-a-01.title: Quadratic residues
pumac-2021-finals-a-01.body: $n^2-n+1\equiv0\pmod p$ with $p$ odd means $(2n-1)^2\equiv-3\pmod p$, so $-3$ is a quadratic residue mod $p$. By quadratic reciprocity $\left(\frac{-3}p\right)=\left(\frac p3\right)$, which equals $1$ only for $p\equiv1\pmod3$. A prime $6k+5$ is $\equiv2\pmod 3$, so $-3$ is a non-residue and no such prime can divide $n^2-n+1$ (the prime $2$ never divides it, and $3$ is not of the form $6k+5$). $\blacksquare$

pumac-2021-finals-a-02.title: Show the circle passes through the arc midpoint
pumac-2021-finals-a-02.body:
Let $X$ be the midpoint of the arc $BD$ of $\Gamma$ containing $A$, and $Y$ the midpoint of the arc $BD$ containing $C$. Both lie on the perpendicular bisector of $BD$, which passes through the center of $\Gamma$, so $XY$ is a diameter. It therefore suffices to prove: **circle $AI_1I_2$ passes through $X$** (the same argument applied to $C$ shows circle $CI_3I_4$ passes through $Y$). If $AB=AD$ then $X=A$ and the statement is the tangency limiting case, so assume $AB\ne AD$, say $p=AB<q=AD$.

*Set-up.* Let $\alpha=\angle BAD$, $a_1=\angle BAE$, $a_2=\angle EAD$ ($a_1+a_2=\alpha$), $k=BE=ED$, $m=AE$. Put $A$ at the origin with the $x$-axis along the internal bisector of $\angle BAD$. Then $B$ lies in direction $-\frac\alpha2$, $D$ in direction $+\frac\alpha2$, $AE$ in direction $-\frac\alpha2+a_1$. Since $AI_1$ bisects $\angle BAE$ and $AI_2$ bisects $\angle EAD$:
$$\text{direction of }AI_1=-\tfrac{a_2}2,\qquad\text{direction of }AI_2=+\tfrac{a_1}2.$$

*Distances.* In a triangle, the distance from a vertex $V$ (angle $\phi$) to the incenter is $\dfrac{s-\text{(opposite side)}}{\cos(\phi/2)}$. In $\triangle ABE$ the side opposite $A$ is $BE=k$, so $AI_1=\dfrac{m+p-k}{2\cos(a_1/2)}$; in $\triangle ADE$, $AI_2=\dfrac{m+q-k}{2\cos(a_2/2)}$.

*The point $X$.* Let $X_0$ be the point on the line through $A$ perpendicular to the bisector (the external bisector), on the $D$-side, with $AX_0=h=\dfrac{q-p}{2\sin(\alpha/2)}$, i.e. $X_0=(0,h)$. Then
$$X_0B^2=p^2\cos^2\tfrac\alpha2+\left(h+p\sin\tfrac\alpha2\right)^2=p^2+h^2+p(q-p)=h^2+pq,$$
and likewise $X_0D^2=q^2+h^2-q(q-p)=h^2+pq$. So $X_0$ lies on the perpendicular bisector of $BD$ and on the external bisector at $A$. The arc midpoint $X$ also lies on both lines (the external bisector of $\angle BAD$ meets $\Gamma$ at the midpoint of arc $BAD$) and these lines meet in one point when $p\ne q$, so $X_0=X$.

*Concyclicity via inversion at $A$.* Invert about $A$ with radius $1$. A circle through $A$ becomes a line, so we must show $I_1',I_2',X'$ are collinear. With $P=m+p-k$, $Q=m+q-k$ and $c=2\cos\frac{a_1}2\cos\frac{a_2}2$:
$$I_1'=\left(\frac{c}{P},\ -\frac{2\cos\frac{a_1}2\sin\frac{a_2}2}{P}\right),\quad I_2'=\left(\frac cQ,\ \frac{2\cos\frac{a_2}2\sin\frac{a_1}2}{Q}\right),\quad X'=\left(0,\ \frac{2\sin\frac\alpha2}{q-p}\right).$$
The line $I_1'I_2'$ meets $x=0$ at height
$$y_1-x_1\frac{y_2-y_1}{x_2-x_1}=-\frac{2}{P(p-q)}\Bigl[\cos\tfrac{a_1}2\sin\tfrac{a_2}2(p-q)+\cos\tfrac{a_2}2\sin\tfrac{a_1}2\,P+\cos\tfrac{a_1}2\sin\tfrac{a_2}2\,Q\Bigr].$$
Since $Q+(p-q)=P$, the bracket equals $P\sin\frac{a_1+a_2}2=P\sin\frac\alpha2$, so the height is $\dfrac{2\sin(\alpha/2)}{q-p}$, exactly the height of $X'$. Hence $I_1',I_2',X'$ are collinear, i.e. $A,I_1,I_2,X$ are concyclic.

*Conclusion.* Circle $AI_1I_2$ meets $\Gamma$ at $A$ and $X$ (the midpoint of arc $BAD$); by the same argument applied to triangle $CBD$ with the same midpoint $E$, circle $CI_3I_4$ meets $\Gamma$ at $C$ and $Y$, the midpoint of arc $BCD$. These are the two midpoints of the arcs cut off by $BD$, hence diametrically opposite. $\blacksquare$

pumac-2021-finals-a-03.title: Reduce to a walk on strings
pumac-2021-finals-a-03.body:
Let $n=2022$ and call a binary string of length $n$ a *state*. Let $V(s)$ be the number of steps Alice can force the game to last, with $V(0^n)=0$ and $V=\infty$ if Bob can prevent the zero string. From $s=r\,x$ ($r$ the first $n-1$ digits, $x$ the last digit) the next state is $0r$ or $1r$; Alice picks if $x=1$, Bob if $x=0$. So
$$V(r1)=1+\min\bigl(V(0r),V(1r)\bigr),\qquad V(r0)=1+\max\bigl(V(0r),V(1r)\bigr)\quad(r\ne0^{n-1}),$$
and $V(0^{n-1}1)=1$ since $0^{n-1}1$ moves to $0^n$ by Alice's choice. Note $r0$ and $r1$ have the same two options $0r,1r$.

**Levels.** Let $L_k=\{s:V(s)=k\}$. We show each $L_k$ has at most one element and describe the sequence. $L_0=\{0^n\}$. Suppose $L_0,\dots,L_{k-1}$ are the singletons $\{s_0\},\dots,\{s_{k-1}\}$. A state of value $k$ is either $r1$ with $\min(V(0r),V(1r))=k-1$ or $r0$ with $\max=k-1$; in both cases $s_{k-1}\in\{0r,1r\}$, so $r$ is the last $n-1$ digits of $s_{k-1}$, and the two candidates are $r0,r1$. If the partner of $s_{k-1}$ (the other state $\bar s$ with the same last $n-1$ digits) has not occurred yet, only $r1$ qualifies ($\min=k-1$); if it has occurred, only $r0$ qualifies ($\max=k-1$). So $L_k$ has exactly one element, namely
$$s_k=\begin{cases}r1&\text{if the partner of }s_{k-1}\text{ is new}\\ r0&\text{otherwise,}\end{cases}\qquad r=\text{last }n-1\text{ digits of }s_{k-1},$$
as long as that state is not already used; this fails only when $s_{k-1}=10^{n-1}$ (then the candidate is $0^n=s_0$), where the process stops.

**This is the prefer-one walk.** The rule says: from $s_{k-1}$, append the digit $1$ on the right (and drop the left digit) unless the resulting window was already visited, in which case append $0$. This is exactly Martin's "prefer-one" construction of a de Bruijn sequence started at $0^n$ (view the states as the $n$-windows of a cyclic binary sequence). By Martin's theorem this greedy walk visits **all** $2^n$ binary strings of length $n$ exactly once, ending at $10^{n-1}$. (One checks directly that $V$ is finite on every state for $n\le10$ by computer, and the first levels for $n=4$ are $0000,0001,0011,0111,1111,1110,1101,1011,0110,1100,1001,0010,0101,1010,0100,1000$.)

**Conclusion.**
a) Every string occurs in the walk, so $V(s)<\infty$ for all $s$: Bob can never prevent Alice from reaching the all-zero string.

b) The values $V(s_k)=k$ are $0,1,\dots,2^{n}-1$, all distinct. The maximum is $2^n-1=2^{2022}-1$, attained only at the last state of the walk, $s_{2^n-1}=1\underbrace{0\ldots0}_{2021}$. So the maximal game time is $2^{2022}-1$ steps and the unique string achieving it is $b=10\ldots0$ (a $1$ followed by $2021$ zeros).

pumac-2021-finals-a-03.title: Small cases
pumac-2021-finals-a-03.body: Solving the game exactly by backward induction for $n=1,\dots,10$ gives maximal game times $1,3,7,15,\dots,1023=2^n-1$, always attained by exactly one string, $10\ldots0$, and finite value for every string. For example for $n=3$ the values $V(000),\dots,V(111)$ are $0,1,6,2,7,5,4,3$, i.e. the order $000,001,011,111,110,101,010,100$, ending at $100$ with $V=7=2^3-1$. This supports the general answer above.
